title: Weak Squares & Holes
subtitle: See the holes in a pawn structure — and occupy them.
goals: Invade holes with the right pieces

steps.say: Every pawn move creates a hole: a square that pawn can never defend again. Black's ...g6 advance left h6 and f6 permanently weak — and with no dark-squared bishop to compensate, those DARK squares around the king are open wounds. Strategy is largely the art of seeing, creating and occupying holes.

steps.prompt: Black's dark squares are defenseless. March your bishop into the hole next to the king!
hints: The g6 pawn can never guard h6 again — and Black's dark-squared bishop left the board long ago.
Bc1–h6: nothing can ever evict the bishop, and it hits f8 on arrival.

line.say: Into the wound! The bishop attacks the f8 rook, owns the dark squares by the king, and no black pawn or piece can ever challenge it. Holes are homes.

rejections.say: A pleasant square — but ...f6 kicks the bishop with tempo. h6 is the true hole: NO black pawn can ever touch it, and from there the bishop hits f8 immediately.

steps.wrongSay: Which dark square beside the king can never be defended by a pawn again? Go there.
steps.successSay: When the enemy weakens one color, pieces of that color become monsters.

steps.prompt: The f6 hole is a knight's dream — and it comes with royal benefits. Jump in!
hints: With Black's g-pawn on g6, the f6 square is a permanent hole — and a knight there touches the king's court.
Nf6+ — check! — and count what else that knight attacks...

line.say: Into the hole with CHECK — and the knight simultaneously attacks the d7 queen!
The queen falls. The hole on f6 wasn't just a nice square — it was a launchpad aimed at the king and everything near him.

rejections.say: It pokes at defended pawns only. The HOLE was f6 — un-defendable, arriving with check, and forking the queen.

steps.wrongSay: The hole in front of the king is reachable right now — with check, no less.
steps.successSay: Holes near the king are worth more than material — they're where combinations are born.

steps.prompt: Dark squares around Black's king: undefended. Your dark-square army: assembled. Send in the queen!
hints: Your Bb2 already owns the long dark diagonal. The queen wants the hole beside the king.
Qh6! The threat is Qg7# — supported by the bishop — and ...f6 fails to your knight.

line.say: The dark squares collapse at once: Qg7# is threatened (the b2 bishop backs it up), the blocking try ...f6 walks into Nxf6+, and no black piece can reach the dark squares in time. A color-complex execution.

rejections.say: Retreating from the battle — the dark squares beg for the QUEEN: from h6 the mate on g7 (backed by your bishop) cannot be met.
Tempting — but after ...Kh8 the knight alone can't finish the job. Send the queen into the h6 hole first; the whole dark-square complex falls at once.

steps.wrongSay: The g7 square is guarded only by the king — and your bishop already stares at it. Which queen move creates unstoppable mate threats?
steps.successSay: Weak squares come in COLORS. Own the color, and every square of it belongs to you at once.

steps.prompt: Black pushed both center pawns past their duties — see the hole they left behind and exploit it!
hints: The d5 and f5 pawns can never guard e6 again. What lands there — and what does it hit?
Ne6: an untouchable fork of queen and rook, sitting in the hole Black dug themselves.

line.say: The hole becomes a gallows — queen and rook forked from a square no black pawn can ever attack!
The exchange is won, and the knight escapes via the very hole it invaded. Every careless pawn push leaves a square like this behind.

rejections.say: Qxd5! A pawn grab straight into the queen's mouth. The real prize was the HOLE those advanced pawns left behind them: e6.

steps.wrongSay: Look at the squares Black's advanced pawns abandoned — one of them forks everything.
steps.successSay: Pawns can't move backward: every advance is a promise. Learn to collect on broken promises.
